stem: A nurse is caring for a client during early recovery after a cesarean birth. Which plan best supports detection and prevention of common postoperative and postpartum complications?

options.A: Assess the incision, uterine fundus, lochia, pain, bowel and bladder function, and extremities; assist with ambulation when clinically appropriate and permitted.
options.B: Focus assessment on the abdominal incision because uterine tone and lochia are not clinically relevant after a cesarean birth.
options.C: Keep the client on bed rest until discharge to protect the incision and avoid provoking postoperative pain.
options.D: Delay incision assessment until discharge teaching unless the client first reports drainage or wound pain.

rationale: A is correct. A client who has had a cesarean birth requires both routine postpartum assessment and additional postoperative assessment. Current NCBI nursing guidance includes evaluation of the uterine fundus, lochia, bladder, bowel function, extremities, pain, and the cesarean dressing/incision. Early ambulation is also encouraged when clinically appropriate because it supports postoperative recovery and circulation. B is incorrect because cesarean birth does not eliminate the risk of uterine atony or postpartum hemorrhage; fundal and lochia assessment remain essential. C is incorrect because routine prolonged bed rest is not recommended and can impede recovery. D is incorrect because the incision is assessed during hospitalization for dressing condition, approximation, and signs of infection rather than only when symptoms are volunteered or at discharge.
educational_objective: After cesarean birth, integrate routine postpartum surveillance with postoperative assessment of the incision, pain, bowel/bladder function, and mobility, and promote ambulation when clinically appropriate to support recovery and reduce complication risk.
source_organization: National Library of Medicine / NCBI Bookshelf
source_document_title: Nursing Health Promotion — Postpartum Care; Health Alterations — Routine Postoperative Nursing Interventions
source_version_date: Nursing Health Promotion 2025 edition and current postoperative nursing text, pages accessed 2026-08-17
source_locator: Nursing Health Promotion, Postpartum Care — BUBBLE-EE Focused Postpartum Assessments: assess fundus, cesarean incision, bladder, bowels, lochia, extremities and emotional status; Uterus section: assess cesarean dressing/incision for cleanliness, approximation and infection; Additional Cesarean Birth Discomforts: encourage early/frequent ambulation to support recovery. Health Alterations, Table 2.5b Routine Postoperative Nursing Interventions: assist out of bed and ambulate as soon as appropriate according to agency policy/provider orders and continue DVT surveillance.
source_claim_supported: Post-cesarean nursing care combines routine postpartum assessment with surgical-incision and postoperative assessment, pain management and clinically appropriate early mobility; fundal and lochia assessment remain necessary after cesarean birth.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing
blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Reduction of Risk Potential: monitor clients for potential complications associated with treatments and procedures, recognize changes in assessment findings, and implement measures that reduce complication risk.
blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — postoperative/postpartum surveillance after cesarean birth
correction_summary: Rebuilt the broad source item into a risk-focused postoperative postpartum plan and corrected the blueprint from Basic Care and Comfort to Reduction of Risk Potential. Removed the unsupported implication that one generic care bundle universally prevents specific complications and qualified ambulation by clinical appropriateness, provider orders, and agency policy.
audit_reviewer: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol — Rule 1 clinical audit + adversarial second pass

audit_findings.clinical_category: post-cesarean recovery / complication surveillance / postoperative mobility
audit_findings.source_audit: Verified current NCBI postpartum and postoperative nursing guidance. The sources directly support incision assessment, continued fundal/lochia assessment, bowel/bladder and extremity assessment, pain care, and early ambulation when appropriate.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: A integrates the source-supported domains without imposing a universal timing threshold. B falsely excludes postpartum uterine/lochia surveillance after surgery. C substitutes prolonged bed rest for recommended mobility. D delays a routine surgical-site assessment until symptoms or discharge.
audit_findings.choice_A: Correct; it combines postpartum and postoperative surveillance with appropriate mobility.
audit_findings.choice_B: Incorrect but plausible siloed-care error; cesarean clients still require postpartum hemorrhage and involution assessment.
audit_findings.choice_C: Incorrect; prolonged routine bed rest is inconsistent with postoperative recovery guidance.
audit_findings.choice_D: Incorrect; incision assessment is part of ongoing inpatient care, not only discharge teaching or symptom-triggered evaluation.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A addresses both obstetric and postoperative risks. The other choices each omit an essential surveillance or recovery component.
audit_findings.cueing: All options are competing post-cesarean care plans of similar scope; the correct answer is not identifiable by a unique emergency term or a numerical cue.
audit_findings.blueprint: The construct is surveillance and prevention of complications after surgery and childbirth, fitting Reduction of Risk Potential rather than routine comfort alone.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Rechecked whether every cesarean client must ambulate at a fixed time or whether VTE prophylaxis is uniform. The final wording avoids fixed timing and medication/device mandates, stating ambulation only when clinically appropriate and permitted. Rechecked incision, fundus, lochia and mobility claims against NCBI sources. No unresolved conflict remained.
